Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis  
Details: The problem arises in the `Frequency` class in method `getPct(Object)`. The deprecated `getPct(Object)` method returns the value of `getCumPct((Comparable<?>) v)`, i.e., a cumulative percentage rather than the intended specific percentage of that value. The correct method to get the percentage of values equal to `v` is `getPct(Comparable<?>)`, which returns the count of that value divided by the total frequency count (`getCount(v) / getSumFreq()`).  

The failing test `testPcts()` expected a call to `getPct(Object)` to return the exact percentage of the value `3` rather than the cumulative percentage up to `3`. However, since `getPct(Object)` delegates to `getCumPct(Comparable<?>)` which returns a cumulative frequency percentage, it leads to an incorrect result that causes the test to fail.  

This issue was pointed out in the bug report summary and description that the use of `getCumPct` in `getPct(Object)` is incorrect and prevents a drop-in replacement from version 1.2 to 2.0 due to behavioral difference. The correct approach is to have `getPct(Object)` delegate to `getPct(Comparable<?>)`.  

The recent bug reports are unrelated to this issue.  

Hence, the bug is caused by the implementation of deprecated `getPct(Object)` incorrectly using cumulative percentage instead of direct percentage. This mismatch causes the test failure when using `getPct(Object)` with an `Object` argument.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
